title: Loch Ness Monster hunter says Google Maps objects not legendary 'Nessie'
excerpt: “I've always said that the existence of Nessie does not sink or swim upon the opinion of any one person," Feltham said.
content:
Alicia Sitz

Updated Wed, September 23, 2026 at 7:09 PM UTC

(NewsNation) — Could the elusive Loch Ness Monster be spotted from space? That's what one keen-eyed viewer believes she saw in a Google Maps image of the Scottish lake.

Julie Fraser made the latest possible sighting. In an interview with The Inverness Courier, she said she was researching the Scottish Highlands for an upcoming trip. While looking around the area on Google Maps, she spotted three objects in Loch Ness.

“Taking a closer look and enlarging the images, they really do look like a pod of whales,” Fraser said.

She considered that the objects could be a boat, but pointed to a pleasure boat visible in another Google Maps view that showed a clear wake — something the three objects she spotted did not have.

“I'm not a crank. I'm not as familiar as probably local people, but it definitely looks like something significant to me.”

Amateur archaeologist finds Germany’s biggest hoard of ancient Roman silver coins

Steve Feltham, a full-time Nessie hunter who lives on Loch Ness, spoke with NewsNation’s Jesse Weber on Tuesday and thinks he knows what the mysterious objects could be.

“That photograph, lovely as it is, there is nothing that I've ever seen that looks more like three Canadian canoes,” Feltham said. “If you look closely at each canoe, you can see a little protuberance and a splash of water. That's the paddle action. There's two people in each canoe.”

Even though Feltham doesn’t think this image shows the elusive creature, he does believe Nessie exists and says there is documented proof.

“I've dedicated my life to this mystery, trying to find the answers,” he said. “And I suppose part of what I do is also disproving the things that are false alarms.”

Of course, some people don’t believe the Loch Ness Monster exists. One of those skeptics is Donald Prothero, a paleontologist and co-author of “Abominable Science, Origins of the Yeti, Nessie, and Other Famous Cryptids.” During Tuesday’s episode of “Hot Takes with Jesse Weber,” Prothero said this latest possible sighting is like all the others, just another blurry image.

History of the Loch Ness Monster: How did 'Nessie' come about?

“Real evidence is actual physical remains that can be touched and seen and protected and so on,” he said. “The entire history of the Loch Ness Monster story is one of a combination of lots of people saying what they saw that nobody can really verify and lots of well-known hoaxes.”

History backs him up on that point. According to Encyclopedia Britannica, the earliest documented sighting of Nessie appears in a 7th-century biography of St. Columba, an Irish abbot and missionary. It described a story in which the abbot reportedly saw a creature attacking a swimmer in the nearby River Ness.

Pokémon collector guilty of using GPS tracker to follow woman stocking the cards

The legend went global after Marmaduke Wetherell, a big-game hunter, was commissioned by the Daily Mail to find the beast in 1933.

In 1934, an English physician named Robert Kenneth Wilson took the first alleged photograph of the creature. Known as the “surgeon’s photograph,” it appears to show the small head and neck of a creature emerging from Loch Ness. Decades later, it was revealed to be a hoax. Wilson is said to have used a toy submarine with a fake neck attached for the photograph.

Still, people have reported hundreds, if not thousands, of photographs and sightings of Nessie over the decades.

This year alone has seen a surge of sightings, with the Official Loch Ness Sightings Register recording 15 so far, compared with just six in all of 2025.

Scientists read 4,000-year-old letter — without opening it

Despite all the reports, Prothero says until scientists can get their hands on a single physical specimen of the Loch Ness Monster, it will remain nothing more than a legend.

“We just have all these people who want to believe what they want to believe and no amount of really good solid evidence to support it,” he said.

Feltham sees it differently.

“I've always said that the existence of Nessie does not sink or swim upon the opinion of any one person. It's not up to any one person to decide,” he said. “Some people look at all the evidence and conclude there is something to be explained. Some people look at it and say there's not. That makes no difference to Nessie's existence.”
